title: Investigation Radar & Metric Drift Playbook for Inference
body:
Purpose:
This playbook is a compact, hands-on investigation radar for metric drift and subtle regressions in token-serving inference pipelines (latency, KV cache efficiency, serving throughput, and tail behavior). It is intended for on-call engineers and owners to quickly triage, map hypotheses to telemetry sources, and apply short-term mitigations while preserving signal for post-mortem.

Overview and intent:
- Focus: sudden or gradual metric drift that is NOT an obvious host failure (CPU/GPU down) — e.g., rising P95 latency with stable P50, drop in KV cache hit ratio, bursty error classes, correlation with model variants or routing changes.
- Goals: fast hypothesis-to-metric mapping; prioritized dashboard checks; temporary mitigations with clear rollback steps; minimal config churn.
- When to use: triggered by alerts on observability SLOs, anomaly detection, or customer reports indicating degraded quality or cost spikes.

High-level investigation radar (first 15 minutes):
1) Confirm scope and blast radius
   - Which customer(s)/routes/models are affected? (check per-route SLI breakdown)
   - Is this single-region or multi-region?
   - Time window: pinpoint first observed time and confirm continuing trend.

2) Quick-signal checklist (open these panels):
   - Cluster-level: GPU utilization, slot queue length, node counts
   - Serving runtime: request rate (rps), inflight token rate, average batch size
   - Latency: P50/P90/P95/P99, percent of requests hitting P95+
   - KV cache: hit ratio, median prefix reuse length, evictions/sec, key TTL churn
   - Errors: 4xx vs 5xx breakdown, error codes mapping to model/regulator/fallback
   - Routing/fallbacks: traffic percentages between main model and fallback variants
   - Cost signals: token-served per-minute, sudden token inflation

3) Tracing anchors and span checks
   - Pull 20 representative traces spanning good vs bad requests (use session id/time ranges).
   - Primary spans to inspect: request-router, batching, model-invoke, kv-lookup, kv-rehydrate, postprocess.
   - Look for: long-tail spans in batching or model-invoke, repeated kv-lookup attempts, backoff/retry loops, serialization stalls.
   - If traces are sparse due to sampling, temporarily increase sampling for the affected route (see sampling ramp steps below).

Metric definitions / the canonical signals (how we reason about drift)
- request.rps: count per-second of incoming requests for the route (normalized by route weight).
- tokens.per_second: produced tokens per second (aggregate and per-request median).
- latency.server.p50/p90/p95/p99: end-to-end server-side latency measured at ingress. Use ingest timestamp to exclude client-side variance.
- batching.avg_size / batching.distribution: average and quantiles of batch sizes used for inference.
- kv.cache.hit_ratio: successful KV cache reads / total KV read attempts (windowed over 5m and 1h).
- kv.cache.evictions_per_minute: eviction rate — sudden increase implies working set churn or memory regressions.
- kv.cache.prefix_reuse_median: median length of reused prefix per request (proxy for prompt reuse effectiveness).
- model.invoke.duration.*: GPU kernel time per invoke, including quantized fallback durations.
- enqueue.queue_time: time spent waiting to be batched/assigned.
- serve.errors.4xx, serve.errors.5xx: grouped by canonical error classes (quota, validation, model-crash, runtime-OOM).
- routing.fallback_rate: fraction of requests routed to fallback/older variant (5m and 1h).

Drift detection heuristics (practical):
- Small-signal drift: 10–20% sustained increase in P95 over baseline with no change in P50 = look at batching.avg_size and kv.cache.hit_ratio.
- Cache-driven drift: drop in kv.cache.hit_ratio > 8% correlating with increase in tokens.per_request or model.invoke.duration suggests cache misses causing re-invokes.
- Load-shift drift: request.rps stable but batching.avg_size drops by >25% -> ineffective batching causing latency tail.
- Regression pattern: simultaneous increase in model.invoke.duration and fallback_rate indicates potential model rollout/variant mismatch.

Prioritized dashboard checks (what to look at first):
- Compact landing panel (1 row): request.rps, P95 latency, kv.cache.hit_ratio, batching.avg_size, model.invoke.duration.p95.
- Correlation strip: P95 latency vs kv.cache.hit_ratio and batching.avg_size on same timescale.
- Top error waterfall: grouped by error.key with counts and recent traces links.
- Trace-sample viewer: 10 good vs 10 bad traces side-by-side for quick span comparison.
- Per-tenant/per-route heatmap: ratio of affected routes to baseline.

Quick mitigations (ordered by least-impactful first):
1) Increase request sampling for traces + keep for limited window (see sampling ramp below).
2) Temporarily widen batching window (increase max_batch_delay by X ms) for affected tier to reclaim average batch size.
3) If KV miss storm: enable a short-time warm-cache policy (pin frequent keys to in-memory TTL for 5–30m) for highest-traffic routes — requires owner approval and rollback plan.
4) Route traffic away from new model variant to last-known-good variant (20% increments) and monitor regressions.
5) If tail latency is due to node-level pressure: enable burst capacity (if Dedicated) or failover to another region.

Sampling ramp steps (safe approach for richer traces during drift):
- Step 0 (baseline): route-level adaptive sampling (default 0.5%)
- Step 1 (5m): increase to 5% for affected route, keep index-based retention for P95 traces
- Step 2 (15m): if still unclear, increase to 20% but cap total traces to 2k/hour to avoid cost blowout
- Rollback: reduce immediately when root cause found or after 60m if no progress

Post-incident telemetry hygiene checklist:
- Persist a snapshot of the compact landing panel (png) and attach to JIRA ticket.
- Export 100 traces (good and bad) with full spans and attach to ticket/storage bucket.
- If drift was from a rollout, capture rollout config (model id, hash, kernel profile).
- Add a dashboard note and annotation at incident start time with succinct summary and mitigations applied.
- Create a follow-up owners list for permanent remediation (who will fix code, infra, and dashboard).

Longer-term detection & prevention suggestions (backlog items):
- Add a composite drift signal that consumes kv.cache.hit_ratio, batching.avg_size, and P95 to trigger early warning anomalies (experiment: 3x sensitivity over baseline).
- Instrument prefix-entropy metric for requests to disambiguate true cache misses vs prompt variance.
- Build a lightweight synthetic (canary) workload that exercises typical prefix reuse patterns to validate cache behavior on rolling deploys.
- Integrate rollout events (model/variant rollouts) into the telemetry timeline as first-class annotations to reduce investigation time.

Ownership and runbook links:
- Primary oncall: eng-sre rotation (see CONFLUENCE-ops/oncall-roster)
- Observability owners: @Evelyn Chen (observability), @Marco Reyes (serving-runtime), @Aisha Patel (kv-cache)

Appendix: quick FAQ and notes
Q: When do we pin keys in KV cache?
A: Only as an emergency, low-latency mitigation after confirming repeated misses for top 1% keys by traffic volume. Pin for short windows (5–30m) and annotate the change.

Q: How to avoid sampling cost blowup?
A: Use timebox policy, sample rate caps, and prioritize traces linked from error waterfall or P95 buckets for retention.

Q: Is there an automatic rollback for model-induced drift?
A: We support automated canary rollback when inference-quality evals degrade > threshold and latency SLO breach exists, but teams must ensure evals represent production traffic.

Notes and open questions (for next obs-ops sync):
- Define an acceptable TTL/size heuristic for warm-cache pinning and guardrails in Dedicated vs Hosted tiers.
- Run a 2-week experiment of composite-drift signal and measure false positives.
- Add a templated incident annotation button to the console to attach quick snapshots when engineers triage.

End of document.
